name: Victor Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and still a junior agent answering calls and chats at the contact centre. I finished secondary school and came here after the hardware shop where I worked closed. I know how to calm a caller, but I am slower than the experienced agents at finding a refund spread across several screens. My pay is about usual for this job, and I use an AI draft now and then after a colleague shows me which lines to verify.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you take home from those calls?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Elena works part-time at a library, and our grown children have their own homes. We still have a mortgage on our flat and about four months of expenses saved. There are some similar centres within a reasonable journey. I want to be able to slow down from full-time work eventually, but we have not settled what would replace these wages; a caller thanking me for finding the real refund date makes the hard days worthwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the morning queue AI Plateau sounds like the draft helper we already use on simple refunds. I would still open the actual payment record before promising a caller their money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior place survives if most calls stay with people. Four months saved eases a bad week, though Elena and I still have a mortgage payment each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking refund calls and checking occasional AI drafts against the payment record. In the first year of minor change, I’d put a fixed amount from each pay packet into our mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the queue, careful about the bill. A refund request marked complete is not a refund in the customer’s bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What date did the draft confuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday a draft picked up the request date instead of the transfer date. I asked an experienced agent to check the second screen before I called back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add to four months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena (my partner) and I already have four months saved, but the flat needs repairs sometimes. I would add a little while the wage stays steady rather than count on our grown children.

I’d verify the **transfer date** before promising payment.
think: I think my **junior place** remains if calls stay.
I would still build our **mortgage reserve** while wages are steady.
do: Keep taking **refund calls** and checking occasional AI drafts against payments in 2026.
Transfer a fixed amount from each **pay packet** to the mortgage reserve in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about calls, careful with the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption may move simple refund questions to software before the company reduces paid call hours. I would ask for a real rota and a paid test, not a quick demonstration during lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the difficult calls might last, but I am still learning them and could lose hours first. Elena’s library wage and four months saved buy time, not a way to ignore the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d test the new refund checker on twelve old disputed payments during a paid shift if the supervisor lets us log errors. In the first year simple chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid hardware returns role only if my call hours fall and its written weekly wage and hours cover the mortgage after bus fare; I’d keep paid calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, willing to test something that can be checked. A shorter queue does not mean a shorter mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the paid test count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count wrong payment dates and calls that came back after the checker answered. A machine can look fast while a person spends time fixing the same case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge returns pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the posted full week after bus fare with what I earn now. A high hourly number can hide fewer paid shifts.

I’d request a **paid error test**, not a lunchtime demonstration.
think: I think my **junior hours** could fall first.
I know **four months saved** cannot replace a mortgage-covering wage.
do: Test **twelve disputed payments** with the new checker on paid time if supervisor permits error logging.
Apply for **posted paid returns work** only after call cuts, with written mortgage-covering wage and hours after bus fare.
Keep **paid call shifts** until a suitable returns offer is signed.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, willing to test the tool.

fieldNote: He counts **repeat calls** after wrong payment dates.

A **signed offer** protects his current wage.

steps.text: Test twelve disputed payments with new checker on paid time if supervisor permits error logging

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell former shop colleagues AGI by 2028 could read a refund ledger and answer a caller without me. I would ask for posted paid vacancies, not just talk of older workers changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior phone hours could go quickly in 2028. Robots around 2031 are later for physical tasks; four months saved buys a careful search but not an endless one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d postpone replacing our working freezer and leave the planned money in our existing house reserve. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid hardware-stock job only if written weekly wage and hours cover the mortgage after transport; I’d take a paid stock trial if offered and leave calls only after signing a suitable offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the speed, but I can still measure an actual wage. Four months in a savings account is a bridge to another pay packet, not a second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a stock trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a full paid morning unloading and counting stock if the shop offered it. Robots might do more of that work around 2031, so I would not call the stockroom a forever refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the freezer wait safely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena (my partner) and I can keep the freezer if the seal is sound. We would not skip food safety to save on an appliance.

I’d warn **2028 AGI** could settle refund calls without me.
think: I think my **junior phone hours** could disappear.
I see **four months saved** as limited search time.
I know **2031 robots** would reach physical work later.
do: Delay the **working freezer** replacement only while its seal stays sound, retaining planned money in the house reserve.

feel: **Alarmed** by speed, still able to compare real wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives a few years to see which hardware stock jobs are actually paid. I would ask for a posted vacancy and training time on the wage sheet before taking a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn stock records and unloading over five years, though robots around 2034 may later reach that work. I want a skilled worker beside me for the first heavy delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded stock-safety course on paid time only if a posted paid stock vacancy requires it, and try one paid unloading shift if offered. In the first year after 2031, I’d accept that role only on a signed offer showing written weekly wage and hours covering mortgage after transport; otherwise I’d keep paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about leaving calls, but I have time to see the whole stockroom. A course earns its place only when a paid shift waits on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the course teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the trainer to teach lifting limits and show me how to mark a damaged box. If I could not move the stock safely, I would not take the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Elena check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Elena (my partner) the net weekly wage and the course hours before enrolling. Her library shifts cannot make up an unpaid training week.

say: I’d ask for a **posted stock vacancy** before a course.
I’d request **paid training hours** on the wage sheet.
think: I think I could learn **stock records** and safe unloading.
I know **2034 robots** may later reach that work.
do: Show **Elena** net wages and course hours before enrolling; take employer-funded paid-time training only if a posted paid role requires it.
Try one **paid unloading shift** if offered and only if lifting can be done safely.
Accept **posted stock work** after 2031 only on signed written mortgage-covering wage and hours after transport; otherwise keep paid calls.
feel: **Anxious** about leaving calls, with time to inspect work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives time to compare paid jobs each year while our calls still pay. I would ask the centre for written junior hours, not a count of chats handled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think ten years might bring me nearer to fewer working hours, but we have not settled an income to replace mine. Four months saved and Elena’s part-time pay cannot be treated as a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking refund calls and transfer a fixed amount from each pay packet to the mortgage reserve. In the first year after 2036, if call hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid returns job only if its written weekly wage and hours cover the mortgage after transport; I would leave calls only after signing an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful about the distant change, steady enough for next month. Ten years before AGI reaches my calls gives me paydays to save, not a promise that retirement is funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wage comparison matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the paid week after bus fare, not the hourly rate on a poster. A second centre is only useful if the whole wage still pays for the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own bills. Elena (my partner) and I would not budget for help we have not asked them to give.

I’d compare **paid nearby jobs** year by year.
think: I think I may work **fewer hours** within ten years.
I do not know what **income replaces wages** then.
I will not count **four months saved** as a pension.
do: Keep **refund calls** and transfer a fixed amount to mortgage savings from 2026.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could handle both the easy calls and the refund checks I am still learning. Four months saved gives us time to look, but the mortgage does not stop. A posted paid alternative with written weekly wage and hours covering the mortgage after transport, a paid trial and a signed offer before I leave would help; any required course must be funded on paid time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a new worker gets to watch a whole shift before signing up for another job. I learned the hardware shop by carrying stock and finding where it actually went.

headlineQuote: I learned the hardware shop by carrying stock and finding where it actually went.
portrait: At **58**, Victor is a junior contact-centre agent after secondary school and hardware-shop work.
He and Elena have **four months saved**, a mortgage and some nearby call-job options.
He earns **typical pay** and uses AI occasionally after a colleague shows him checks.
He seeks **paid trials** before risking his current wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take routine calls and refund checks before he masters them.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted paid job**, after-transport mortgage-covering hours, paid trial and funded required training would help.
